text: This is a walkthrough of version one. What you're seeing is a wireframe. It shows what each screen does and how the work moves through it, not the final look. We'll follow one job, from the first estimate to the paid invoice.

A customer calls about wrapping two vans. The owner starts an estimate and adds each van from a saved package. One click pulls in every line, with cost and price on each line, and the margin for each van. Unit 17 is a longer van, so the owner adds more film, and the price updates.
Inside the shop, the estimate stays itemized. Switch to the customer view, and each van becomes a single line with one price. Same estimate, two audiences.
The customer approves one van now and holds off on the second. The owner records who approved, when, and how, and records the deposit.
From the approved estimate, the owner clicks Create job. It lands on the job board, where every active job moves through its stages. When printing starts, the owner drags it into production.

Now the technician's side, on a phone. Technicians only see the jobs assigned to them, and never see costs or profit. They clock in for the day, open the job, and start a timer. Only one timer runs at a time, so hours can't be counted twice. When the install is done, they add completion photos and send it for review.

Back at the desk, the job is still in installation in progress, marked needs review. The owner reviews the photos and the estimated against actual hours, and closes the job. It moves to completed, and closing it creates the draft invoice.

One line per vehicle, the deposit already taken off, and the customer's other unpaid invoices listed underneath. The owner emails it straight from the system, with the PDF attached and a pay-by-card link. When the customer pays, the balance updates on its own, and the invoice goes to QuickBooks.
At the end of each pay period, the owner reviews timesheets, approves them, and exports the hours for payroll. Clocked hours and job time are kept separate, so nothing gets paid twice.

Graphics is the first division, but it's built on the same foundation the repair shops can move onto later. Each division can use its own words and stages. Graphics calls the work a job. A repair shop could call it a service order, with repair stages instead. In version one, only graphics is set up.
And here's what version one does not include. Live inventory counts, a customer portal, and the repair shops themselves come later, built on top of this. Leads and texting stay in GoHighLevel.
That's version one. Graphics runs completely off FullBay, on a foundation the rest of the company can grow into.
